question_interpretation: Asks what content a 510(k) premarket notification submission must contain under current regulations.

issues.detail: J lists only 807.87(a), (b), (c), (e), (f), (h). It omits other mandatory 807.87 contents: (d) action taken to comply with section 514 performance standards; (g) supporting data for a significant change/new indication; (i) financial certification or disclosure statement under part 54; (j) statements on compliance of clinical investigations with parts 50/56/812 (or 812.28 for foreign data); (k) class III summary and certification for pre-1990 class III predicates; (l) truthful-and-accurate statement.

explanation: G (807.87) is the governing section and every element in J is supported by it. question_interpretation: Asks for the legal standard for substantial equivalence (SE) and how FDA makes the SE determination for a 510(k).

issues.detail: J omits the core finding required for a device with different technological characteristics: the data must demonstrate the device is 'as safe and as effective as' a legally marketed device (807.100(b)(2)(ii)(B); FD&C Act 513(i)(1)(A)(ii)(I)). 'Supporting performance data' does not state the standard.

'How it is determined' is not answered: FDA compares the device to a legally marketed predicate and issues an order (SE/NSE, request additional information) under 807.100(a); the predicate must not have been removed from the market by FDA or judicially found misbranded/adulterated (807.100(b)(3); 513(i)(2)).

explanation: G correctly pairs the regulation (807.100) with the statutory definition (513(i)). J captures the intended-use and technological-characteristics prongs but drops the 'as safe and as effective as a legally marketed device' showing and the predicate/FDA-order mechanics that the question's second half asks for.
proposed_corrected_answer: SE (FD&C Act 513(i)(1)(A); 21 CFR 807.100(b)) means, compared with a legally marketed predicate, the device has the same intended use AND either (i) the same technological characteristics, or (ii) different technological characteristics, where the submitted information (including clinical data if FDA deems it necessary) demonstrates the device is as safe and as effective as a legally marketed device and does not raise different questions of safety and effectiveness. The predicate must not have been removed from the market at FDA's initiative or judicially determined misbranded/adulterated (807.100(b)(3); 513(i)(2)). FDA determines SE by reviewing the 510(k) and issuing an order declaring the device SE or NSE, requesting additional information, or withholding a decision pending part 54 certification (807.100(a)); the device may not be marketed until an SE order is received.

question_interpretation: Asks when a PMA supplement is required after approval, and when a 30-day notice may be used instead.

issues.detail: 'Real-time supplement option' does not appear in 814.39 or anywhere in Part 814. The term is defined in FD&C Act 737(4)(D) (21 U.S.C. 379i(4)(D), a user-fee definition) and its procedure is in FDA guidance. A key that requires it while citing only 814.39 forces answers beyond G.

J omits other 814.39 routes: changes that don't affect safety or effectiveness, or that are consistent with an approved PCCP, go in periodic reports (814.39(b)); the Special PMA Supplement—Changes Being Effected (814.39(d)); and the 30-day PMA supplement FDA designates by advisory opinion or correspondence (814.39(e)), which is distinct from the 30-day notice.

30-day notice (814.39(f)): only for modifications to manufacturing procedures or methods of manufacture that affect safety and effectiveness. The notice must describe the change, summarize supporting data, and state the change was made under part 820. Distribution may begin 30 days after FDA receipt unless FDA finds the notice inadequate, in which case a 135-day PMA supplement is required. J's 'certain manufacturing process changes' is a loose paraphrase.

explanation: 814.39 is the right section and J's first two elements match 814.39(a) and (f). The 'real-time supplement' element is not supported by the cited regulation; it comes from the user-fee statute and guidance. J also leaves out the CBE, 30-day PMA supplement, periodic-report and PCCP routes that 814.39 itself provides.
proposed_corrected_answer: After PMA approval, a PMA supplement must be submitted and approved before any change affecting safety or effectiveness (e.g., new indications, labeling, facility, sterilization, packaging, design/specification changes, expiry extension under an unapproved protocol) (814.39(a)). Exceptions: changes not affecting safety or effectiveness, or consistent with an approved PCCP, may be reported in periodic reports (814.39(b)); certain safety-enhancing labeling and QC changes may be implemented on receipt acknowledgment of a 'Special PMA Supplement—Changes Being Effected' (814.39(d)); FDA may designate changes for a periodic report or a 30-day PMA supplement (814.39(e)). A 30-day notice (814.39(f); FD&C Act 515(d)) is permitted for modifications to manufacturing procedures or methods of manufacture that affect safety and effectiveness: it must describe the change, summarize supporting data and state the change was made under part 820, and the device may be distributed 30 days after FDA receipt unless FDA finds the notice inadequate and requires a 135-day PMA supplement. (Real-time supplements are a user-fee/guidance category defined in FD&C Act 737(4)(D), not in 814.39.)

question_interpretation: Asks what the De Novo classification process is and what a De Novo request must contain.

issues.detail: J covers content only partially and leaves out the process: the two entry routes (after an NSE determination, or directly when no predicate exists; 860.200(b), 513(f)(2)(A)(i)-(ii)); FDA acceptance review within 15 days (860.230); decision by written order within 120 days (860.240(a), 513(f)(2)(A)(iii)); grant or decline grounds (860.260); Federal Register notice within 30 days of a grant; and the granted device becoming a predicate (513(f)(2)(B)(i)).

Key content items in 860.220(a) are not reflected: classification summary/search for a predicate (a)(8), device description (a)(6), indications (a)(5), classification recommendation (a)(11), nonclinical/clinical/software technical sections (a)(15), and labeling (a)(18).

explanation: G (860 Subpart D; 513(f)(2)) is correct. J's elements (classification into class I or II, risks and mitigations, benefit-risk, proposed special controls) are supported by 860.200/860.220(a)(9), (10), (14). J does not describe the process half of the question and omits much of the required content.
proposed_corrected_answer: De Novo (FD&C Act 513(f)(2); 21 CFR 860 Subpart D) is a request for classification into class I or II of a low-to-moderate-risk device for which there is no legally marketed predicate. It may be submitted after an NSE 510(k) determination or directly where the requester determines no predicate exists (860.200(b)). The request must be electronic and signed (860.210). It must contain (860.220(a)): administrative information and regulatory history; device name, indications for use and description; alternative practices; a classification summary (predicate searches, or the NSE 510(k)); a summary of risks and proposed mitigations (general and, for class II, special controls); an initial draft of proposed special controls for class II; a class recommendation with rationale; relevant standards; study summaries; a benefit-risk discussion based on valid scientific evidence; nonclinical, software and clinical technical sections; bibliography; samples on request; and labeling. FDA decides acceptance within 15 days (860.230) and issues a grant or decline order within 120 days (860.240(a)). A grant is published in the Federal Register within 30 days with any special controls (860.260(a)(2)), and the device becomes a predicate (513(f)(2)(B)(i)).

question_interpretation: Asks how devices are classified into classes I/II/III and what a section 513(g) request for information does.

issues.detail: 860.84 covers only the original classification of preamendments devices and expressly excludes devices placed in class III by statute under 513(f)(1). New (postamendments) devices are automatically class III unless found SE, granted De Novo, or reclassified (513(f)(1)). Neither G nor J mentions this, though it is how most new devices are classified.
J omits the 513(g) mechanics: a written request by any person, with FDA providing a written statement of the classification (if any) and applicable requirements within 60 days.
The class definitions are statutory in 513(a)(1)(A)-(C) and regulatory in 860.3. Classification regulations by device type are in parts 862-892 (860.3, 'Classification regulation').

explanation: 860.3 is correctly cited for class definitions and general/special controls, and 513(g) is correctly identified. But 860.84 alone gives a misleading picture of 'how devices are classified', because it is limited to preamendments devices and excludes statutory class III. J also leaves out the 60-day written response that defines what a 513(g) request produces.
proposed_corrected_answer: Devices are placed into class I (general controls sufficient), class II (general controls insufficient; special controls can provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness) or class III (insufficient information for I/II, and life-supporting/sustaining, of substantial importance in preventing impairment of health, or presenting a potential unreasonable risk; requires PMA), based on the controls needed for reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness (FD&C Act 513(a)(1); 21 CFR 860.3). Preamendments device types were classified by regulation on classification-panel recommendations (860.84); classifications are codified in parts 862-892. A postamendments device is class III by operation of law unless it is substantially equivalent to a class I/II or preamendments predicate, classified through De Novo, or reclassified (513(f)(1)-(3)). Under 513(g), any person may submit a written request for information on a device's classification and the FD&C Act requirements that apply to it. Within 60 days FDA provides a written statement of the classification (if any) and the applicable requirements.

question_interpretation: Asks when an IDE (FDA-approved application) is required for a device clinical investigation, and what makes a device 'significant risk'.

issues.detail: The operative 'when is an IDE application required' rule is 812.20(a)(1)-(2): a sponsor must submit an application to FDA if it intends to use a significant risk device, conduct an investigation with an exception from informed consent under 50.24, or if FDA notifies it, and may not begin until FDA approves. 812.20 is not in G.

J does not state the significant risk criteria the question asks for. Under 812.3(m)(1)-(4), an SR device is an implant, a life-supporting/sustaining device, or one of substantial importance in diagnosing, curing, mitigating or treating disease, in each case presenting a potential for serious risk to health, safety or welfare; or a device that otherwise presents such a risk.
The IRB's role in SR/NSR determinations (812.2(b)(1)(ii); 812.66) and the specific abbreviated-requirements conditions in 812.2(b)(1)(i)-(vii) are not cited or described.

explanation: G is partly right (812.2 and 812.3(m) are correct pinpoints). J is only a topic list ('SR vs NSR determination, abbreviated requirements, exempt investigations') and does not state the SR criteria the question asks for. The section that triggers an IDE application (812.20(a)) is missing.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 812 applies to all clinical investigations of devices to determine safety and effectiveness (812.2(a)), except exempt investigations listed in 812.2(c): preamendment and SE devices used per labeling, certain noninvasive diagnostics, consumer preference/modification testing not for safety and effectiveness, veterinary, laboratory-animal and custom devices. A sponsor must submit an IDE application and obtain FDA approval before starting if the investigation uses a significant risk device, involves a 50.24 exception from informed consent, or FDA so requires (812.20(a)). A significant risk device (812.3(m)) is an investigational device that presents a potential for serious risk to the health, safety or welfare of a subject and (1) is intended as an implant, (2) is for supporting or sustaining human life, (3) is for a use of substantial importance in diagnosing, curing, mitigating or treating disease or otherwise preventing impairment of health, or (4) otherwise presents such a risk. Non-significant risk investigations are considered to have an approved IDE if the sponsor meets the abbreviated requirements in 812.2(b)(1): labeling, IRB approval after an NSR explanation, informed consent, monitoring, limited records/reports, and no promotion. If the IRB disagrees and finds SR, it notifies the investigator/sponsor (812.66).

It also omits obtaining signed investigator agreements (812.43(c)), shipping only to qualified investigators (812.43(b)), selecting qualified monitors (812.43(d)), immediately evaluating unanticipated adverse device effects and terminating unreasonable-risk investigations within 5 working days of the determination and 15 working days of first notice (812.46(b)), and the 812.7 prohibitions on promotion.

question_interpretation: Asks who must register device establishments and list devices, and the timing for initial and annual registration/listing.

Only annual registration and annual listing review fall between October 1 and December 31 (807.22(b)(1), (b)(3)).

Timing omissions: registration information changes are due within 30 days (807.22(b)(2)); listing changes may be made at other times (807.22(b)(4)); foreign establishment listings must be submitted before import, and US agent changes reported within 10 business days (807.28(c), 807.40(b)(3)).

Most of J is supported, but its phrasing assigns initial registration to the October-December window, which is inconsistent with the 30-day rule in 807.22(a), and its 'fees' element has no basis in the cited regulations (it comes from FD&C Act 738). question_interpretation: Asks what Part 803 requires for written MDR procedures and for MDR files/recordkeeping.

issues.detail: Retention is stated imprecisely. Manufacturers and importers keep MDR event files for 2 years from the date of the event or the expected life of the device, whichever is greater. User facilities keep them for 2 years from the event only (803.18(c)). J's 'two years or expected device life' omits 'whichever is greater' and the user-facility distinction.

J omits other 803.17 procedure elements: timely transmission of complete reports (a)(3) and documentation/recordkeeping procedures (b)(1)-(4). It also omits MDR event file contents (803.18(b)(1): deliberations and decisions on reportability, copies of reports, FDA electronic acknowledgments), FDA access (803.18(b)(2)), and the distributor complaint-record obligation with its own 2-years-or-expected-life retention (803.18(d)).

explanation: 803.17 and 803.18 are the governing sections and J's procedural elements are verbatim-accurate. The retention element is materially imprecise: it lacks the 'whichever is greater' rule and does not note that user facilities keep records for 2 years only. Other recordkeeping content is also omitted.
proposed_corrected_answer: Every user facility, importer and manufacturer must develop, maintain and implement written MDR procedures (803.17) for internal systems that provide (1) timely and effective identification, communication and evaluation of events that may be subject to MDR; (2) a standardized review process for determining reportability; and (3) timely transmission of complete reports. The procedures must also cover documentation and recordkeeping of the information evaluated, the reports submitted, annual-report information, and systems ensuring access for FDA follow-up and inspection. Each must establish and maintain clearly identified MDR event files (803.18). These contain the information or references considered, documentation of reportability deliberations and decisions, copies of all reports and related submissions, and FDA electronic acknowledgments, and must be open to FDA access. Retention: user facilities keep files for 2 years from the event; manufacturers and importers for 2 years from the event or the device's expected life, whichever is greater, even if the device is no longer distributed (803.18(c)). Distributors keep device complaint records for 2 years or the expected life, whichever is greater (803.18(d)). Manufacturers may keep MDR event files in the part 820 complaint file (803.18(e)).

question_interpretation: Asks what 21 CFR Part 7 (Subpart C) provides on recall classification and firm-initiated recalls.

issues.detail: The class I/II/III definitions are at 7.3(m)(1)-(3), and G's '7.3' is acceptable but unpinpointed. Recall classification is assigned by FDA after an ad hoc committee health hazard evaluation (7.41).

Part 7 Subpart C is titled 'Guidance on Policy, Procedures, and Industry Responsibilities' and 7.40 describes recall as voluntary. A firm-initiated recall is 'requested' to notify FDA (7.46(a)). An answer should not present these as mandatory, though J does not say they are. For devices, mandatory correction/removal reporting is in Part 806.

explanation: G (7.3, 7.41, 7.42, 7.46) covers the asked topics and every J element is supported: class definitions (7.3(m)), health hazard evaluation (7.41), recall strategy with depth, public warning and effectiveness checks (7.42(b)), and firm-initiated recall notification (7.46). No element misstates the text. The voluntary/guidance character and the 7.3(m) pinpoint are noted for answer quality only.

question_interpretation: Asks how Part 7 distinguishes a recall, a market withdrawal and a stock recovery.

issues.detail: Market withdrawal also covers removals/corrections involving no violation (e.g., normal stock rotation), per 7.3(j). The stock recovery test is that the product has not been marketed or has not left the firm's direct control, with no portion of the lot released for sale or use (7.3(k)). For devices, Part 806 has parallel definitions (806.2(i), (m)) and exempts both from 806 reporting (806.1(b)).

explanation: The pinpoints 7.3(g), 7.3(j) and 7.3(k) are the correct paragraph letters for recall, market withdrawal and stock recovery, and J's three contrasts track the text. The omission of 'or no violation' from the market-withdrawal summary is minor.

evidence.quote: (g) Recall means a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that the Food and Drug Administration considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action, e.g., seizure. Recall does not include a market withdrawal or a stock recovery.
evidence.issuing_authority: eCFR / Office of the Federal Register & GPO

evidence.quote: (j) Market withdrawal means a firm's removal or correction of a distributed product which involves a minor violation that would not be subject to legal action by the Food and Drug Administration or which involves no violation, e.g., normal stock rotation practices, routine equipment adjustments and repairs, etc.
evidence.issuing_authority: eCFR / Office of the Federal Register & GPO

evidence.quote: (k) Stock recovery means a firm's removal or correction of a product that has not been marketed or that has not left the direct control of the firm, i.e., the product is located on premises owned by, or under the control of, the firm and no portion of the lot has been released for sale or use.
evidence.issuing_authority: eCFR / Office of the Federal Register & GPO

rubric_fairness: fair — pinpoints and elements match 7.3.
